The record describes an algorithmic system that scores or profiles individuals to guide a healthcare decision — for example, flagging which patients are at higher risk of complications so care can be prioritized. Algorithmic health-risk profiling of this kind is the class of processing California's significant-decision rules address (11 CCR §§ 7001(ddd)(5), 7200(a)). Italy's data protection authority (Garante) confronted a similar fact pattern when it fined a Friuli-region health authority €55,000 for using an algorithm and patients' own data to build risk profiles without a valid legal basis for that specific use, and without completing the data protection impact assessment the processing required. The aggravating factor the regulator cited was the number of people affected — this was not a one-off, isolated use. This decision was decided under the GDPR, not California's ADMT rules, so it is persuasive only here; whether it applies to this company depends on what this company's own system actually decides, what legal basis supports the profiling, and whether the required assessments were completed first. (Garante per la protezione dei dati personali (Italian Data Protection Authority), Azienda Universitaria Friuli Occidentale, decision of 15 December 2022; foreign supervisory-authority decision, cited by analogy — decided under the GDPR, not the CCPA or its Article 10/11 regulations.)
